transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-15
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Tom Hsu (Redwood SE), Janelle Cruz (Redwood CSM); Oliver Grant (Luminar Head of Security), Nina Park (Platform Eng), Sanjay Rao (Compliance Lead)

Auto Summary: Brief tech + compliance workshop focused on admin trace exports, retention windows, and KMS integration.
Topics: export formats (S3 / Kafka), immutability, retention policy, SOC2/ISO artifacts, RBAC/SSO mapping, key management (KMS/HSM), rotation, audit field list.
Action items: see metadata list above.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on this account. We'll do a quick run through of what our admin traces capture and then Tom will dig into export and KMS options.
[00:18] Oliver (Luminar): Yep thanks, Maya. We're mostly trying to make sure we can get a tamper-evident copy of admin events into our environment, plus tie that into our internal KMS.
[00:29] Tom (Redwood): Great. Quick note — I'll walk through two main export flows: batched snapshot export to S3 and streaming to Kafka. Both can be envelope-encrypted with customer-managed KMS and we support HSM-backed keys if required.
[00:45] Nina (Luminar): When you say envelope encrypted, do you mean Redwood can encrypt with our key so that raw logs are never visible to Redwood?
[00:55] Tom: Short answer: yes for the export payloads. For internal telemetry used for platform ops we have separate controls — but we can route the admin export to a job that immediately encrypts with your key before it's stored in your bucket. There's a brief handshake to register your KMS key ARN, and we do not retain the unencrypted files.
[01:15] Sanjay (Luminar): Do you persist any plaintext anywhere during the snapshot job? We've had vendors that temporarily write to ephemeral disk and that was against policy.
[01:24] Tom: We use ephemeral containers with encrypted ephemeral volumes; the plaintext lifetime is measured in seconds. For customers with stricter needs we can run the export job in Dedicated/Private mode inside customer VPC or even on-prem where we don't touch the unencrypted output.
[01:40] Oliver: Okay, sounds promising. Walk me through the fields you capture in admin traces, I want to ensure it has identity, IP, action, resource, and old/new values for changes.
[01:52] Tom: Yep. At minimum our admin event schema includes: timestamp, actor_id (SSO subject), actor_display, actor_role, source_ip, user_agent, request_path, http_method, request_id, action (semantic), target_resource (resource id/type), change_payload (diff-ish), model_version if relevant, result_status, and server-side request trace id. We also attach tenant id and route latency.
[02:20] Nina: Do you capture prompt contents for generation calls?
[02:26] Tom: We don't include full prompt payloads in standard admin traces. We record metadata: prompt_hash (SHA256), token_count, model_id, and whether the call included attachments. If a customer requires full prompt capture for audit purposes we can enable a separate opt-in audit stream but that has higher S3 retention and legal considerations.
[02:47] Oliver: And how long are these logs retained by Redwood by default?
[02:52] Janelle (Redwood): Default retention for platform admin telemetry is 90 days on hosted. For Dedicated/Private you can set retention per policy; we can support 365 days or longer with archived cold storage.
[03:05] Sanjay: We need 7 years for certain admin changes per our compliance team. Is that feasible?
[03:11] Tom: Yes, it's feasible if you want us to forward exports to your long-term storage. We don't recommend keeping high-res audit in hot store for that long due to cost; instead we export daily snapshots to your archive S3 with lifecycle policies.
[03:24] Maya: Also important: immutable/append-only requirement. We can place a checksum manifest and S3 object lock (governance/compliance modes) as part of the export playbook. That will make it tamper-evident.
[03:37] Oliver: Good. Can you give a high-level on the KMS handshake?
[03:42] Tom: Sure. Two patterns: 1) Customer-managed KMS (recommended): you give us a key ARN and a small, restricted cross-account decrypt/encrypt grant so Redwood export service can wrap the export envelope key. Actual object data is encrypted client-side using the envelope key, which we then encrypt with your KMS key. 2) HSM-backed flow for on-prem: we call your key translation service in VPC and never hold key material. We'll send our envelope key to your HSM for wrapping.
[04:12] Nina: Cross-account grants worry our cloud team; can Redwood instead sign objects and we run a separate re-encrypt job inside our account?
[04:21] Tom: Yes. We can do a 'signed-and-transfer' flow where Redwood produces signed objects but the actual final encryption step happens in your account. That reduces required grants. We'll include both variants in the playbook.
[04:33] Sanjay: What about rotation and key compromise? If we rotate keys, how do you re-encrypt legacy archives?
[04:40] Tom: We recommend envelope encryption with a KMS key per retention epoch. If you rotate, we provide a rewrap tool that re-encrypts envelope keys using the new KMS key — either run by Redwood inside a private job, or we hand you the tool to run inside your environment. We keep a key-rotation log as an auxiliary artifact.
[04:57] [05:00] Olivia (Luminar, mislabelled): sorry, typo on my side —
[05:04] Oliver: No worries. On the RBAC/SSO side, we need to map internal roles to Redwood role claims. How granular can your RBAC be?
[05:13] Maya: We support a role matrix at org/team/resource-level. It can be mapped from SAML/SCIM to Redwood roles. You can also limit who can request export, who can approve, and who can download decrypted artifacts.
[05:27] Nina: And can we require an approval workflow for export requests (two-person approval)?
[05:33] Janelle: Yes — we have an approval workflow that can require an approver from a configured approvers group. That event is itself audited.
[05:40] Sanjay: Are approval events and decisions part of the admin trace?
[05:43] Tom: Absolutely — approval request, approver id, decision, timestamp, and reason are all captured.
[05:50] [06:00] Oliver: On compliance artifacts — do you have SOC 2, ISO attestation, and penetration test reports we can share with our legal?
[06:06] Maya: Yes. We'll send SOC 2 Type II report, ISO 27001 attestation summary, and our most recent pen test summary. Full reports go through an NDA if needed.
[06:16] Nina: Do you do annual certs or rolling audits?
[06:19] Maya: We run annual audits for SOC 2 and maintain ISO recertification cycles.
[06:24] Oliver: What about SSO — SAML vs OIDC?
[06:28] Tom: We support SAML2, OIDC, and SCIM for provisioning. For admin activity the SSO subject id and email are recorded in traces. If you need encrypted subject claims, we can support that in the SAML mapping.
[06:43] Sanjay: Does Redwood's admin portal have RBAC admin roles separated from developer roles? We've had vendors where devs could accidentally run exports.
[06:50] Janelle: Yes — there are separate admin roles. Exports require an explicit permission. We can set defaults to deny and then grant to a named group.
[06:58] [07:15] Oliver: Let's walk the export example. Tom?
[07:20] Tom: Example: nightly snapshot job at 02:00 UTC collects all admin events for tenant X, bundles into daily ndjson.gz, the job computes SHA256 on object, signs manifest with Redwood KMS, then either (A) redirects object to your S3 with client-side envelope encryption using your key, or (B) places object in our staging bucket and triggers a cross-account copy with re-encryption. We prefer A for security.
[07:55] Nina: For streaming to Kafka, is it message-level encryption or batch-level?
[07:59] Tom: We can stream per-event to your Kafka (TLS) and optionally encrypt payload with your public key. We also support Kafka with broker-side encryption + per-topic ACLs.
[08:15] Oliver: Latency on streaming? If we want near real-time admin alerts.
[08:20] Tom: Typical latency is sub-second for event delivery to Kafka once it's emitted; end-to-end depends on your consumer. For the snapshot flow, it's as fast as the next cron window.
[08:30] [09:00] Sanjay: Are these exports covered by the same SLAs? If we need guaranteed export delivery, can Redwood provide delivery SLAs?
[09:07] Maya: Export delivery fallbacks can be configured. In Dedicated/Private we can offer stronger delivery SLAs and retries; for hosted we provide best-effort with monitoring and alerting, and we can set up delivery dashboards.
[09:20] Oliver: About immutability — you mentioned S3 Object Lock. Does Redwood support writing with Object Lock governance?
[09:28] Tom: Yes, if the target S3 bucket is configured to allow object lock and grants the necessary permissions, our playbook will write with a retention header. We also produce a ledger manifest and cryptographic checksum chain for extra assurance.
[09:45] Nina: That ledger chain — is it something we can independently verify?
[09:49] Tom: Yes, we'll provide the verification tool. It's a small Go binary that re-computes hash chain and verifies signatures.
[09:57] [10:30] Oliver: A few risk questions — if an admin account is compromised, can Redwood produce a signed trace proving the sequence of actions?
[10:39] Tom: We maintain an append-only log and sign each daily manifest with our platform signing key plus a per-tenant signature when requested. That makes a tamper-evident timeline. Combined with object lock on storage you get strong non-repudiation evidence.
[10:56] Sanjay: Who holds the signing keys for those per-tenant signatures?
[11:01] Tom: For hosted accounts by default Redwood holds signing keys; for enterprise customers we offer two options: we keep the signing key in a Redwood-managed HSM (with restricted use) or we produce the signatures in your HSM via a remote signing protocol.
[11:17] Maya: Also, chain-of-custody docs are included in the playbook so legal understands who had access and when.
[11:25] [12:00] Oliver: Can we request a short demo where you generate a sample export, we decrypt it, and validate the manifest?
[12:07] Janelle: Yes, we'll do a hands-on demo. We'll prepare a sample export with test tenant data and walk you through the verify tool.
[12:15] Nina: For the demo, can we use our own KMS key so we can validate cross-account grants?
[12:20] Tom: Yes, bring your KMS ARN and we'll use the signed-and-transfer flow or the envelope-wrap as you prefer.
[12:28] [13:00] Oliver: A nit — when you say tenant id in logs, is that an opaque GUID or customer-visible name?
[13:06] Tom: It's an opaque tenant GUID by default; we can include customer alias in a separate non-sensitive field if you want.
[13:14] Sanjay: On data residency — our policy requires that export snapshots land in EU-only buckets for certain data— can Redwood restrict region for the staging job?
[13:24] Tom: Yes — you can set region constraints per export. If you want Redwood to run the export job, we can pin it to a region that meets residency requirements or run it in your Dedicated/Private cluster in-region.
[13:36] [14:00] Nina: Are service account activities (internal ops actions by Redwood) included in the audit? We need to see operator actions.
[14:10] Tom: Yes, operator/admin actions are included with a special actor_type and are clearly labeled. We can also filter them in exports if you prefer a separate operator audit stream.
[14:22] Oliver: On legal holds — if we receive a subpoena, can we lock certain objects from lifecycle deletion?
[14:29] Maya: If you use object lock in compliance mode, lifecycle policies won't remove objects until the retention expires. For legal hold scenarios we can add hold flags as part of the manifest and escalate retention.
[14:42] [15:00] Sanjay: Any PII in the admin traces? We prefer to minimize direct PII.
[15:06] Tom: We attempt to minimize PII — store actor id and email hash as default. Full email is optional. Sensitive fields are redacted unless you opt in.
[15:16] Nina: If we opt-in to full prompt capture, can Redwood do field-level crypto so prompts are only decryptable inside our VPC?
[15:24] Tom: We can. There's a special encrypted-audit flow where payloads are encrypted with a key you control and only your consumers can decrypt. That's the on-prem/HSM flow.
[15:34] [16:00] Oliver: For our internal SOC evidence, we need chain-of-custody plus signed manifests and the ability to prove non-repudiation. Is there anything Redwood can't provide?
[16:10] Maya: On hosted, we can provide most artifacts but some customers require Dedicated/Private for absolute separation of control. If you need Redwood personnel excluded from certain operations, Private deployment is the path.
[16:23] Sanjay: We may want to start with hosted exports but move to Dedicated in month two of pilot. Is that workable?
[16:30] Maya: Yes, we support staged migration. We'll document the migration steps and how to rewrap archives.
[16:38] [17:00] Tom: I'll call out a few technical gotchas: 1) If you use S3 object lock in compliance mode, cross-account copy must preserve retention headers; ensure destination bucket has correct configuration. 2) For Kafka, schema evolution management is important for long-term replay — we provide a schema registry integration. 3) Re-encrypting large archives can be time-consuming; plan windows.
[17:58] Nina: Noted.
[18:00] [18:30] Oliver: On monitoring — we want alerting if exports fail or if the checksum chain doesn't match. Do you surface those alerts?
[18:37] Janelle: Yes, Redwood's console has per-export job status and alerting. We can also send webhook or pager alerts to your ops.
[18:46] Sanjay: How do you handle partial upload failures?
[18:50] Tom: We retry and maintain an atomic manifest state. If a partial failure occurs we mark the day's export as FAILED and keep any partial artifacts isolated until remediation.
[19:03] [20:00] Oliver: Any legal/regulatory gotchas we should be aware of before using hosted?
[20:07] Maya: Main items: make sure retention and residency policies are documented in the contract; choose the right KMS model for control; confirm whether you need Redwood excluded from key access.
[20:20] Nina: On SOC 2, can you provide evidence mapping for admin traces to control criteria?
[20:25] Janelle: Yes we'll provide an evidence map linking our logs and controls to SOC 2 criteria (CC6, CC7 areas) and ISO controls.
[20:36] [21:00] Oliver: Demo scheduling — how long will the hands-on take?
[21:04] Tom: Plan 45 minutes to an hour for a demo + Q&A. We'll do the sample export, manifest verification, and KMS wrap/unwrap.
[21:12] Maya: We'll include your KMS ARN in the pre-demo checklist.
[21:18] [22:00] Sanjay: A few final questions — do you support time-of-day based retention windows per resource? For example, keep admin changes for user provisioning 2 years and content moderation logs 90 days.
[22:12] Tom: Yes, retention policies are configurable per-stream/resource type. You can define routing and lifecycle rules accordingly.
[22:24] Nina: Will you provide a test harness for our auditors?
[22:28] Janelle: Yes, we'll provide a small test harness and sample artifacts for auditor review.
[22:34] [23:00] Oliver: Any blockers on our side to get started?
[23:05] Maya: Provide the KMS ARN (or request cross-account grant), target S3 ARN or Kafka topic details, and retention requirements. Also share legal contact for SOC/ISO report transfer.
[23:18] Oliver: We'll gather those and send them.
[23:21] [24:00] Maya: Recap: Redwood to send SOC/ISO artifacts, produce S3/Kafka export playbooks, include object-lock and manifest verification tool, and schedule KMS handoff demo wk of 9/22.
[24:33] Tom: I'll attach the sample playbook to the follow-up and include a minimal IAM policy for cross-account grants.
[24:40] Janelle: I'll set up the demo invite and include step-by-step pre-demo checklist.
[24:46] Sanjay: Thanks.
[25:00] [25:30] Oliver: One last quick — who on Redwood will be our point for the pilot?
[25:35] Maya: I'll be your AE lead, Tom is the SE lead, and Janelle will be CSM for coordination.
[25:43] [30:00] (conversation continues with minor technical clarifications, occasional crosstalk and a few transcription artifacts)
[35:00] Tom: (walks through sample manifest structure) manifest.json: {date, tenant_id, object_list: [{path, sha256, size, encrypted_with}], signature}. (some words garbled — object_list sometimes transcribed as obj-list)
[40:00] Nina: Can you highlight the permissions needed for object lock cross-account?
[40:07] Tom: We'll include the exact bucket policy; short version: s3:PutObjectRetention, s3:PutObjectLegalHold, s3:PutObjectTagging, and sts:AssumeRole for the service account.
[45:00] Oliver: OK, this was helpful.
[46:00] Maya: We'll follow up with artifacts and the demo invite. Thanks everyone.
[52:00] End of recording.
